title: What the Heap Order Does Not Give You
quickIdea: The heap order constrains parent-child pairs only, so a heap cannot be searched, its inorder walk is not sorted, and the maximum of a min-heap is somewhere among its leaves, which is Theta(n) away.
remember: Only parent-child pairs are ordered; siblings and the two subtrees are free, so there is no branch to follow when looking for an arbitrary key. A search is Theta(n).

The maximum of a min-heap, and the minimum of a max-heap, lies on a leaf. There are ceil(n/2) leaves, so finding it costs Theta(n), and it cannot be done faster because the leaves are unordered among themselves.
Rank bounds that do hold: in a max-heap the k-th largest sits at depth at most k-1, so it lies among the first 2^k - 1 positions; in particular the second largest is a child of the root.
An inorder walk of a heap is not sorted, so a heap is not a BST. A BST becomes a heap in Theta(n); a heap becomes a BST only by paying a sort, Theta(n log n).

Uses that need the extreme over and over: Dijkstra and Prim, Huffman coding, k-way merge, top-k with a heap of size k (Theta(n log k)), median maintenance with one max-heap and one min-heap, and event simulation.
Sorted output costs the sort: n extractions are Theta(n log n), which is the comparison-sort lower bound, so no heap trick beats it.

example.prompt: A min-heap holds 1000 distinct keys. What is the cost of finding the minimum, of finding the maximum, and of finding the third largest of a max-heap on the same keys?
example.work: The minimum is A[1], one step. The maximum is one of the leaves: there are 500 of them, and they are in no order among themselves, so a scan of 499 comparisons is needed in the worst case, which is Theta(n). For the third largest of a max-heap, the rank bound says its depth is at most 2, so it is among indices 1 to 7, and six comparisons settle it.
example.answer: Minimum O(1); maximum Theta(n); third largest O(1), because only the first seven positions can hold it.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2006 Q.10 and GATE CSE 2021 Set 2 Q.2 ask the same fact from opposite sides: the smallest key of a max-heap, and the largest key of a min-heap. In both the distractor is O(log n), which would be right only if the order constrained more than parent-child pairs.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2006 Q.10. In a binary max heap containing n numbers, the smallest element can be found in time (1) O(n) (2) O(log n) (3) O(log log n) (4) O(1)
variations.why: In a max-heap every parent is at least its children, so the smallest key must be a leaf: if it had a child, that child would be smaller. There are up to ceil(n/2) leaves, unordered among themselves, so every one must be inspected, which is Theta(n). Converting the max-heap into a min-heap first would cost Theta(n) as well and buys nothing.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2021 Set 2 Q.2. Let H be a binary min-heap consisting of n elements implemented as an array. What is the worst case time complexity of an optimal algorithm to find the maximum element in H? (1) Theta(1) (2) Theta(log n) (3) Theta(n) (4) Theta(n log n)
variations.why: The maximum of a min-heap is a leaf, and with 1-based indices the leaves are floor(n/2)+1 to n. Scanning those about n/2 cells is Theta(n), and it is optimal because the leaves carry no order among themselves. Binary search over the leaves is not available: they are not sorted.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: A max-heap holds 1000 distinct keys. How many array positions can hold the third largest key?
variations.why: The k-th largest key has at most k-1 ancestors, all larger than it, so its depth is at most k-1. For k = 3 the depth is at most 2, and the positions at depth 0, 1 and 2 are indices 1, 2-3 and 4-7, seven in all. Reading those seven and taking the third largest is O(1) work, which is why top-k questions on a heap are cheap while an arbitrary search is not.

trap.what: Assuming the second largest key is the right child of the root, or that a heap supports O(log n) search because it looks like a tree.
trap.why: The order says nothing about which child is larger, and nothing about cousins. The second largest is one of the root's children but not a named one, and an arbitrary key has no ordered path to follow.
trap.counterexample: [9,8,4,7,6,1,3] is a max-heap whose second largest key, 8, is the left child; the right child holds 4. And the smallest key, 1, sits at index 6, deeper than the larger key 3 at index 7, so no downward rule finds it.

check.question: A max-heap holds 1000 distinct keys. What is the worst-case cost of finding the smallest key, and of finding the third largest?
check.answer: Theta(n) for the smallest, O(1) for the third largest.
check.explanation: The smallest is a leaf, and there are 500 leaves in no order, so the scan is Theta(n). The third largest lies at depth at most 2, hence among indices 1 to 7, so seven reads decide it. The gap between these two answers is the whole content of the heap's partial order.
